provenance.note: Disconfirmation probe (machine-permitted-where-proof-is-scarce). The DET 'uses AI extensively for test design (e.g., automated generation of test items), measurement (e.g., item parameter estimation and automated scoring of written and spoken responses), and test security'. D1=2: Goal 4 requires documenting AI for validity argument, item creation, calibration and scoring, incl. 'explainable scoring methods'; public Transparency Report. D2=1: Accountability & Transparency principle, but 'This document should not be relied upon or considered legally binding, and may be revised by Duolingo at any time.' No named human accountable per score. D3=1: AI use documented publicly; no per-score labeling. D4=1: test-taker identity verification against impersonation. D5=1: humans are in the loop for item review and proctoring ('Human-in-the-loop AI proctoring protocols require proctor rubrics'), but scoring is validated statistically in aggregate: 'Human raters score writing and speaking samples to build a scored data set against which AI models can be evaluated.' Appeals exist only 'where there is suspicion of test-taker misconduct', not for scores. D6=2: validity-argument framing throughout. c2_fit=partially: the human is reserved for misconduct accusations (identity and behavior, where evidence is contestable per case) while the individual proficiency score — a latent construct with no per-person ground truth — is machine-issued and checked only statistically. That permits machine judgment where individual proof is scarce; it fits only if aggregate statistical validation counts as 'cheap proof'.
